content.title: 3 takeaways from Iowa State basketball's Sweet 16 loss to Tennessee
content.text: Updated March 28, 2026, 6:12 a.m. CTCHICAGO — There wasn't anything sweet about Friday night.Iowa State men's basketball had another season brimming with promise and Final Four potential altered by a devastating injury.Undersized and short-handed without All-American Joshua Jefferson, who missed his second straight game with a sprained ankle, No. 2 seed Iowa State fell to sixth-seeded Tennessee on March 27 at United Center. The Volunteers led for a majority of the contest and knocked out the Cyclones, 76-62."Very good team, certainly the better team tonight," Iowa State coach T.J. Otzelberger said of the Volunteers. "On the other side, really proud of our group. For us, we aim every night to lay it on the line. I feel like our guys do that every night. Proud of our team. Our performance tonight doesn't diminish anything we accomplished this season, and really proud of this group. Been as enjoyable group to be around as I've ever had. Tough to have it come to an end."Tennessee's imposing size and unrelenting play were present from opening tip. The Volunteers held a 34-33 halftime lead.The Volunteers pushed the margin into double figures while Iowa State had a five-minute drought in between made shots midway through the second half.The Cyclones managed to trim the deficit to eight with 4:01 remaining, but the Volunteers shut the door on any hopes of a comeback.Iowa State finished the season at 29-8 overall. It was the Cyclones' third Sweet 16 appearance in five years.Tamin Lipsey and Nate Heise each had 18 points, five rebounds and a steal. Lipsey also added five assists.For Tennessee, Nate Ament had 18 points, four boards, three assists and two blocks. Ja'Kobi Gillespie chipped in 16 points. Felix Okpara had a 12-point, 10-rebound double-double, with three blocks and a steal. Jaylen Curry added an 11-point, 10-rebound double-double off the bench.Here are three takeaways from the Cyclones' season-ending loss:Tennessee's big men, overall size overpowered Iowa StateThe Volunteers entered Friday's Sweet 16 game as the top offensive rebounding team in the country. With a rotation that features three starters that are 6-foot-10 or taller, and two tough 6-foot-8 forwards off the bench, Iowa State's task of dealing with that sheer size became even more challenging without Jefferson.The biggest eye-popping difference in a physical contest came on the glass. Tennessee lived up to its reputation and outrebounded Iowa State, 43-22. The Volunteers tallied 16 offensive rebounds, which they converted into 14 second-chance points."We knew that it would be a tremendous challenge," Otzelberger said of Tennessee's size. "I think the most important thing when it comes to rebounding is that you stay in front of the play defensively, guard the dribble, stay out of rotation. ... They've got tremendous size, athleticism and commitment to the glass. They're the best offensive rebounding team in the country, and it certainly proved true tonight."Tennessee's formidable size also made things difficult for the Cyclones on offense.Although the Volunteers turned the ball over 17 times, they were able to mitigate some of the Cyclones' damage by holding them to 14 points off turnovers.Tennessee often got back in transition, but in the half-court the Volunteers were able to use their length to make inside looks difficult. They were also able to disrupt some perimeter or mid-range shots, forcing the Cyclones to attempt more fadeaways and off-balance shots or shoot contested 3-pointers.Milan Momcilovic was held to six points on 2-of-9 shooting, and the Cyclones struggled to get any momentum from the 3-point line. They shot 5-of-23 (21.7%) from deep.The Cyclones' long-range struggles forced Iowa State to try to go inside at times, but nothing came easy.Iowa State shot 38.9% for the game, which was the Cyclones' third-lowest shooting percentage as a team this season."Definitely hurt us a little bit, as far as shots around the rim," guard Jamarion Batemon said of Tennessee's length. "We kind of went away from it because of how much length and kind of settled for shots, so it definitely affected that. It did affect perimeter shots sometimes, where shots you could usually get off, we kind of couldn't sometimes."Iowa State basketball's Tamin Lipsey, Nate Heise leave it all on the court in final gameIowa State seniors Tamin Lipsey and Nate Heise didn't go down quietly. The seniors finished with a team-high 18 points apiece in the loss. They were the only Cyclones to score in double figures.Heise stepped in for Jefferson in the starting five. The versatile two-way guard had 14 of his 18 points in the first half.Although he had been with the program for only two seasons, Heise quickly ingrained himself as a glue guy and a versatile guard who could be plugged into any lineup or situation.A six-year player, the former Northern Iowa Panther appeared in a total of 162 games throughout his career. At Iowa State, he played in 72 games, starting 12, and was a go-to player off the bench."Growing up I never really thought I would be a Division I basketball player, and then I went to UNI," Heise said. "Then I never thought I would be a high-major player, and then I came here. Just the opportunities coach has given me, I couldn't be more grateful to him and then the other coaches along with him. The guys I've gotten to know here, I've had so many good memories outside of basketball, playing the game with them. I just can't be more grateful."As for Lipsey, he had 11 of his 18 points in the second half. He also finished with five rebounds and five assists.A beloved four-year starter, the hometown hero played in 137 games as a Cyclone. He wrapped up his career with 1,507 points, 518 rebounds, 602 assists and a school-record 314 steals."That's a perfect word to use, grateful," Lipsey said. "Just for the whole experience, whole basketball career. Obviously hoping to continue to play, but just looking back on my four years, it was a quick four years. I loved every second of it, the highs, the lows. All of it made me a better player, a better person. Thanks to T.J. and the coaches and how the program is ran."I think Heise and I can say we left it in a better place than we came in."Iowa State star Joshua Jefferson unfortunately doesn't get final curtain callTears fell down Jefferson's cheeks in the postgame locker room. The typically stoic, straight-faced senior couldn't hide his emotions as the Cyclones' season — and his college career — came to a close."It's just hard, when you work so hard to get to a certain point and then something like last week happens, it's really unfortunate," Jefferson said. "I just wish I could be out there with them, just fight with them one last time."Jefferson had worked diligently with trainer Vic Miller and other medical staff to rehab and treat his ankle to potentially get himself in position to play.Despite their best efforts daily, Jefferson revealed that he was never close to making a return."Not even close, just started to jog," Jefferson said. "A lot of pain with it. Probably wouldn't have been able to go Sunday (if Iowa State advanced to the Elite Eight) either, so it was just hard — trying so hard to get out there and physically can't do it."Jefferson never got the send-off or final game he envisioned. The second-team AP All-American entered the NCAA Tournament averaging 16.9 points, 7.6 rebounds, 4.9 assists and 1.7 steals per game. Just minutes into the Cyclones' first-round win over Tennessee State, he suffered a bad ankle sprain after attempting and making his first shot of the game. That was his last play as a Cyclone.Iowa State's second-round win over Kentucky and its loss to Tennessee in the Sweet 16 were the only two games Jefferson had missed since joining the Cyclones for the 2024-25 season."The message is appreciation for everything he's done for our program," Otzelberger said. "What a tough blow to be dealt. You're in the NCAA Tournament, you dream of being there your whole life, you get there, and you have the team that you think can really make a run, and then to have a fluke thing happen where he goes down and then his ankle."Just a really tough circumstance to deal with, so we just wanted to make sure that Joshua felt supported, and we did everything in our power to get him ready to be out there and play. It just wasn't enough."Eugene Rapay covers Iowa State athletics for the Des Moines Register. Contact Eugene at erapay@gannett.com. Follow him on Twitter at @erapay5.
